prime.problem: Walking (1, 1) back to (10⁹, 3) one subtraction at a time takes 333,333,335 steps; float slopes for Max Points divide by zero and collide at 0.9999999894638303; counting magical numbers one by one takes 2 × 10¹³ checks. One idea, replacing many subtractions by a remainder, fixes all three.
prime.fits: Third maths card. It is the purest case of the overview's "take a remainder instead of subtracting", and it sets up modular inverses (extended Euclid) for the next card.
expect: gcd(a, b) = gcd(b, a mod b)
prime.goal: Run Euclid by hand, explain why the remainder keeps the common divisors, and use gcd, lcm and mod to turn long walks into a few steps.

attend: Why does anything dividing a and b also divide a − q·b?
Why does Reaching Points have exactly one parent per point, and why does that allow a backward walk?
Why does dividing (dx, dy) by their gcd and fixing the sign give one exact key per line?
Why is the magical-number count subtracting multiples of the lcm, and why can you binary-search on it?

must: A common divisor of a and b divides a − q·b for any q → replace a by a mod b without changing the common divisors → repeat until 0 → at least halves the smaller number every two steps → O(log min(a, b))

Reaching Points: coordinates stay positive → the bigger one must have been the sum → exactly one parent → walk backwards, and many identical subtractions collapse into one % → 1 loop round instead of 333,333,335
Integer directions divided by their gcd with a fixed sign → exact, hashable keys → no division by zero on vertical lines, no float collisions
Multiples of a or b below x: x//a + x//b − x//lcm (inclusion–exclusion) → count(x) never decreases → binary search the smallest x with count ≥ n → 45 halvings instead of 2 × 10¹³ checks
elevated: Consecutive Fibonacci numbers are Euclid's worst case (Lamé) → gcd(89, 55) takes 9 steps → the log bound is tight
reference: the source's float estimate inside the last lcm block
empty stubs: Self Crossing, Perfect Rectangle, Largest Palindrome Product

compress.prompt: From memory, trace gcd(1071, 462), say in one sentence why each step preserves the gcd, and write the one-line backward step of Reaching Points.
checklist: any common divisor of a and b divides a − q·b
Reaching Points: if tx > ty, tx %= ty, else ty %= tx
stop when a coordinate matches the start, then check divisibility

retrieve.q: Explain why Euclid's algorithm terminates in O(log min(a, b)) steps.
answer: after a step, the pair is (b, a mod b) with a mod b < b
if a mod b > b/2 then the next remainder is < b/2; either way the smaller number halves within two steps

retrieve.q: Walk (3, 5) back to (1, 1) with the Reaching Points loop, then explain the final divisibility check.
answer: tx = sx = 1, so the rest must be y += 1 moves: sy ≤ ty and (2 − 1) % 1 = 0 → True

retrieve.q: For Max Points on a Line, compare float slopes, (dy, dx) reduced by gcd, and pairwise cross-products: correctness and cost.
answer: float slopes: divide by zero on verticals and collide for close slopes
gcd-reduced keys: exact, O(n²) with one counter per anchor
cross products: exact too, but O(n³) if you test every triple; needed for float coordinates with a tolerance

compare.q: Nth Magical Number counts multiples of a or b with inclusion–exclusion. What is the "overlap" term here, and why does the formula grow to 2<sup>k</sup> − 1 terms for k divisors?
answer: the overlap is multiples of both, i.e. of lcm(a, b), counted twice without correction
for k divisors every nonempty subset contributes ± x // lcm(subset)
2<sup>k</sup> − 1 subsets: fine for 2 or 3, not for 20

compare.q: Reaching Points could be searched forwards with BFS. Why is walking backwards so much cheaper, and what change to the moves would force you back to a search?
answer: forwards each point has two children, so the tree doubles per level
backwards each point has one parent, so it's a single path, compressed by %
adding moves like (x, y − x) gives several parents: a general graph, so BFS

predict.q: Predict how many remainder steps Euclid takes for gcd(240, 46) and what the gcd is, before computing.
predict.answer: 5 steps, gcd 2: 240 = 5·46 + 10, 46 = 4·10 + 6, 10 = 1·6 + 4, 6 = 1·4 + 2, 4 = 2·2 + 0. Both numbers are even and 240 / 2 = 120 and 46 / 2 = 23 share no factor, so 2 is right.

apply.task: Write extended Euclid (return g, x, y with a·x + b·y = g) and run it on (1071, 462). Then test reaching_points on (3, 3) → (12, 9) and (1, 1) → (2, 2), and nth_magical(5, 2, 4), explaining each answer.
apply.done: Extended Euclid gives 21 = 1071·(−3) + 462·7. (3, 3) → (12, 9) is True (12 % 9 = 3, then (9 − 3) % 3 = 0); (1, 1) → (2, 2) is False (gcd 2 ≠ 1). nth_magical(5, 2, 4) = 10: every multiple of 4 is already a multiple of 2.
apply.hint: Recursive form: g, x, y = ext(b, a % b); return g, y, x − (a // b)·y.
